summary: The note explains global dimming, the decline in sunlight reaching Earth's surface observed from the 1950s to the 1980s, attributed mainly to sulfate aerosols from industrial pollution. It describes the subsequent partial brightening after the 1980s, its effects on the hydrological cycle, monsoons and temperature, and its relevance to climate projections and solar geoengineering such as stratospheric aerosol injection.
one_line: Global dimming is the decline in sunlight reaching Earth's surface caused largely by aerosol pollution, its partial reversal, and its effects on climate and geoengineering.
key_facts: Global dimming is a decline in the amount of sunlight reaching the Earth's surface, also known as global direct solar irradiance.
Observed reduction in sunlight was 4–5% per decade over late 1950s–1980s, and 2–3% per decade when the 1990s were included.
Solar radiation at the top of the atmosphere did not vary by more than 0.1-0.3% during the dimming period, suggesting the causes were on Earth.
Global dimming had been widely attributed to sulfate aerosols from post-war industrialization.
After 1990, the global dimming trend clearly switched to global brightening due to air pollution controls in developed nations.
In the United States, total emissions of the six principal air pollutants dropped by 53% from 1970 to 2005, according to the EPA.
Global dimming has counteracted some greenhouse gas warming, with the most-polluted regions experiencing cooling in the 1970s.
In the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, sulfate aerosols are believed to offset around 0.5 °C (0.9 °F) of warming.
Black carbon is estimated at about 0.1 °C (0.18 °F) of warming in the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report.
The eruption of Mount Pinatubo in 1991 temporarily reversed the brightening trend.
Aircraft contrails were estimated in 1992 to have an overall warming effect between 3.5 mW/m and 17 mW/m.
Reduced air traffic during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic showed no significant response of diurnal surface air temperature range from contrail changes.
Aerosols are believed to have contributed to the failed monsoon behind the 1984 Ethiopian famine, though the extent of anthropogenic versus natural influence is disputed.
Stratospheric aerosol injection is a solar geoengineering approach that would transport sulfates into the stratosphere, where they would last for years instead of weeks.
Scientific estimates suggest cooling the atmosphere by 1 °C through stratospheric aerosol injection would cost at least $18 billion annually (at 2020 USD value).

entities.name: Atsumu Ohmura
entities.role: Geography researcher at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology who found solar radiation striking the Earth's surface declined by more than 10% over three decades

entities.name: Mount Pinatubo
entities.role: Volcano whose 1991 eruption temporarily reversed the brightening trend and served as an analogue for stratospheric aerosol injection

entities.name: Clean Air Act (United States)
entities.role: US law passed in 1970 and strengthened in 1977 and 1990 that reduced sulfate aerosols

entities.name: Helsinki Protocol on the Reduction of Sulfur Emissions
entities.role: 1985 European measure under the Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution to reduce sulfur emissions

entities.name: IPCC Sixth Assessment Report
entities.role: Report estimating sulfate aerosols offset around 0.5 °C of warming

entities.name: IPCC First Assessment Report
entities.role: 1990 report that acknowledged human-made aerosols may lower temperatures and estimated dimethyl sulfide emissions

entities.name: IPCC Second Assessment Report
entities.role: 1995 report that confidently assessed the overall impact of aerosols as negative (cooling)

entities.name: Mikhail Budyko
entities.role: Suggested in 1974 that the planet could be cooled by burning sulfur in the stratosphere

entities.name: Paul Crutzen
entities.role: Author of the seminal 2006 paper advocating stratospheric aerosol injection

entities.name: Mount Agung
entities.role: Volcano in Bali whose 1963 eruption caused observed atmospheric temperature reductions

entities.name: El Chichón
entities.role: Volcano in Mexico whose 1982 eruption caused observed atmospheric temperature reductions

entities.name: Nevado del Ruiz
entities.role: Volcano in Colombia whose 1985 eruption caused observed atmospheric temperature reductions

entities.name: Stratospheric aerosol injection
entities.role: Solar geoengineering intervention that aims to counteract global warming by releasing reflective aerosols into the stratosphere

entities.name: Sahel drought
entities.role: Drought linked to a failed monsoon in sub-Saharan Africa during the 1970s and 1980s and associated famine

entities.name: 1984 Ethiopian famine
entities.role: Famine behind which multiple studies connected record particulate pollution in the Northern Hemisphere to monsoon failure

entities.name: 2020 coronavirus pandemic
entities.role: Global event that reduced global air traffic by nearly 70% relative to 2019, used as a natural experiment

entities.name: September 11 attacks
entities.role: Event after which no commercial aircraft flew across the USA, widening the diurnal temperature variation
